sections.title: Explaining Matter: Models, Patterns, and the Periodic Table
sections.description:
This seminar explores how scientists explain patterns in the physical world using the periodic table as a central organizing model. Rather than surveying chemical facts, students investigate why elements exhibit recurring trends in properties such as size, reactivity, and electronegativity, and how these trends can be understood through increasingly sophisticated models. Emphasis is placed on scientific reasoning as an iterative process: asking questions, evaluating competing explanations, interpreting qualitative and quantitative data, and determining when simple models are sufficient or when more complex approaches are required. The course also examines how elemental properties shape real-world phenomena, including biological function, toxicity, materials, and environmental systems, highlighting the broader relevance of chemical knowledge.
Through collaborative, inquiry-based activities, students will analyze patterns across the periodic table and connect atomic-level structure to observable properties of matter. Throughout the semester, students will develop their ability to communicate scientific ideas clearly to non-specialist audiences using the Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) framework, culminating in an individual project that applies course concepts to an element of their choice.
Designed for students with a wide range of prior experience in STEM, the seminar emphasizes discussion, collaboration, and the development of transferable approaches to knowledge, including evidence-based reasoning, quantitative interpretation, and interdisciplinary thinking.
